exercises.title: U2 听力·对话 Ordering Food in America
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Lily: Do you want to order some French fries with me?
Tom: French fries? I have no idea what they are.
Lily: They're just hot, thin pieces of potato. You call them chips, right?
Tom: Oh, so your fries are my chips! That's confusing.
Lily: Wait until you hear this. My biscuits are sweet, but yours are salty.
Tom: Salty biscuits? In England a biscuit is always sweet.
Lily: I know. In America, what you call biscuits, we call cookies.
Tom: The same language, but so many different words. How funny!
exercises.translation_cn: Lily 问 Tom 要不要点 French fries;Tom 不知是什么;原来美式 fries 就是英式 chips;biscuit 在美式里是咸的,英式里是甜的;美式的 biscuit 英式叫 cookie;同一语言却用词不同,很好笑。

questions.stem: What does Lily want to order?
What does Tom call "French fries"?
How are biscuits different in their two countries?
options: American ones are salty, British ones are sweet.

questions.stem: What do Americans call what the British call "biscuits"?
How does Tom feel about the differences?

exercises.title: U2 听力·短文 Gestures Around the World
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Using gestures to show feelings is common in some countries but not in others.
Most people think shaking the head means "no".
But in a few places, the same gesture can mean the opposite.
A traveller who is not careful may send the wrong message.
So it is wise to learn how local people use their hands and heads.
exercises.translation_cn: 用手势表达感受在一些国家很常见,在另一些则不然;大多数人以为摇头表示'不';但在少数地方,同样的手势可能表示相反的意思;不小心的旅行者可能传递错误信息;所以最好了解当地人如何使用手和头部动作。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Gestures can mean different things in different countries.

questions.stem: What do most people think shaking the head means?
What can happen to a careless traveller?
options: They may send the wrong message.

questions.stem: In a few places, the head-shaking gesture can mean what?
What does the speaker say is wise to do?
options: Learn how local people use gestures.

exercises.title: U2 听力·对话 What Do You Mean by "Pants"?
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Anna: I really need to buy some new pants this weekend.
Ben: Pants? You usually buy those by yourself, don't you?
Anna: What? I just want someone to tell me if they look nice on my legs.
Ben: On your legs? Do you mean trousers?
Anna: Yes! In American English, pants means trousers.
Ben: Ah, that explains it. In British English, pants means underwear.
Anna: No wonder you looked so surprised just now!
Ben: Don't worry. It's only two ways of speaking the same language.
exercises.translation_cn: Anna 说周末要买 pants;Ben 觉得奇怪;原来 Anna 说的是穿在腿上的;Ben 问她是不是指 trousers;美式英语里 pants 指裤子;英式英语里 pants 指内裤;难怪 Ben 一脸惊讶;这只是同一语言的两种说法。

questions.stem: What does Anna want to buy?
Why is Ben surprised at first?
In American English, what does "pants" mean?
In British English, what does "pants" mean?
How does Ben describe the difference?
options: Two ways of speaking the same language.

exercises.title: U2 听力·短文 The Word "Chi"
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: The simple Chinese word "chi" means "to eat".
But it often goes far beyond its literal meaning.
"Chi cu" sounds like eating vinegar, yet it means to be jealous.
"Chi moshui" sounds like eating ink, but it means to receive an education.
So learners should not always take such a word literally.
exercises.translation_cn: 汉语词'吃'意为 to eat;但它常常超出字面意思;'吃醋'听起来像吃醋,实际指嫉妒;'吃墨水'听起来像吃墨,实际指受教育;所以学习者不应总按字面理解这样的词。

questions.stem: What does the word "chi" basically mean?
What does "chi cu" really mean?
What does "chi moshui" actually mean?
What does the speaker advise learners to do?
options: Not always take the word literally.

questions.stem: What do these examples show about the word "chi"?

exercises.title: U2 听力·对话 A New Sense of Time
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Mia: You've lived in Mexico for years. Has anything about you changed?
Carl: Yes. My attitude towards time has changed a lot.
Mia: What do you mean?
Carl: Back home, I used to panic if I was even five minutes late.
Mia: And now?
Carl: Now I'm still on time for important appointments, but I don't worry so much.
Mia: So you feel more relaxed?
Carl: Exactly. Ironically, I feel I live more in the present moment than before.
exercises.translation_cn: Mia 问在墨西哥住了多年的 Carl 有什么变化;Carl 说他对时间的态度变了很多;以前迟到五分钟都会慌;现在重要约会仍准时,但不太担心了;变得更放松;具有讽刺意味的是,他比以前更活在当下。

questions.stem: What about Carl has changed?
How did Carl feel about being late before?
What is Carl still careful about?
options: Being on time for important appointments.

questions.stem: How does Carl feel about time now?
What does Carl say he does more now?
options: He lives more in the present moment.

exercises.title: U2 听力·短文 Where "Ciao" Comes From
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Many friendly greetings have a surprising history.
The Italian word "ciao" is used to say hello or goodbye.
Long ago, it came from a phrase that literally meant "I am your slave".
Of course, no one takes it that way today.
Its real meaning now is warm and friendly.
exercises.translation_cn: 许多友好的招呼语有令人惊讶的来历;意大利语 'ciao' 用来打招呼或告别;很久以前它来自一个字面意为'我是你的奴隶'的短语;当然今天没人那样理解;如今它的真实含义是温暖友好的。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
When is the word "ciao" used?
What did the original phrase literally mean?
How do people understand "ciao" today?
What does this example show about words?
options: Their meanings can change over time.
